Superior lobe of left lung.summary: The lungs are the primary organs of the respiratory system in many animals, including humans. In mammals and most other tetrapods, two lungs are located near the backbone on either side of the heart. Their function in the respiratory system is to extract oxygen from the atmosphere and transfer it into the bloodstream, and to release carbon dioxide from the bloodstream into the atmosphere, in a process of gas exchange.

Superior medial genicular artery.title: Medial superior genicular artery

fields.Branches: Branch to vastus medialis, branch to surface of the femur and the knee-joint

Superior medial genicular artery.summary: The medial superior genicular artery is a branch of the popliteal artery. It runs deep to the semimembranosus, semitendinosus, and tendon of the adductor magnus, and superior to the medial head of the gastrocnemius. It divides into two branches, one of which supplies the vastus medialis, anastomosing with the highest genicular and medial inferior genicular arteries; the other ramifies close to the surface of the femur, supplying it and the knee-joint, and anastomosing with the lateral superior genicular artery.

Superior mesenteric artery.title: Superior mesenteric artery

fields.Branches: Inferior pancreaticoduodenal; middle colic; right colic; intestinal branches (jejunal, ileal); ileocolic Marginal artery of the colon

Superior mesenteric artery.summary: In human anatomy, the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) is an artery which arises from the anterior surface of the abdominal aorta, just inferior to the origin of the celiac trunk, and supplies blood to the intestine from the lower part of the duodenum through two-thirds of the transverse colon, as well as the pancreas.

Superior mesenteric vein.title: Superior mesenteric vein
Superior mesenteric vein.summary: In human anatomy, the superior mesenteric vein (SMV) is a blood vessel that drains blood from the small intestine (jejunum and ileum). Behind the neck of the pancreas, the superior mesenteric vein combines with the splenic vein to form the portal vein that carries blood to the liver. The superior mesenteric vein lies to the right of the similarly named artery, the superior mesenteric artery, which originates from the abdominal aorta.

Superior oblique muscle.title: Superior oblique muscle

fields.Origin: Sphenoid bone at the orbital apex, medial to optic canal
fields.Insertion: Outer posterior quadrant of the eyeball
fields.Blood supply: Lateral muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery
fields.Action: Primary action is intorsion (medial rotation); secondary actions are to abduct and depress the eyeball (i.e. it makes the eye move outward and downward)

Superior oblique muscle.summary: The superior oblique muscle or obliquus oculi superior is a fusiform muscle originating in the upper, medial side of the orbit (i.e. from beside the nose) which abducts, depresses and internally rotates the eye. It is the only extraocular muscle innervated by the trochlear nerve (the fourth cranial nerve).

Superior occipital gyrus.title: Occipital gyri
Superior occipital gyrus.summary: The occipital gyri (OcG) are three gyri in parallel, along the lateral portion of the occipital lobe, also referred to as a composite structure in the brain. The gyri are the superior occipital gyrus, the middle occipital gyrus, and the inferior occipital gyrus, and these are also known as the occipital face area. The superior and inferior occipital sulci separates the three occipital gyri.

Superior ophthalmic vein.title: Superior ophthalmic vein

fields.Source: Union of angular vein and supraorbital vein

Superior ophthalmic vein.summary: The superior ophthalmic vein is a vein of the orbit that drains venous blood from structures of the upper orbit. It is formed by the union of the angular vein, and supraorbital vein. It passes backwards within the orbit alongside the ophthalmic artery, then exits the orbit through the superior orbital fissure to drain into the cavernous sinus.

Superior parathyroid gland.title: Parathyroid gland

fields.Latin: glandula parathyreoidea inferior, glandula parathyreoidea superior
fields.Develops from: Neural crest mesenchyme and third and fourth pharyngeal pouch endoderm
fields.Blood supply: Superior thyroid artery, inferior thyroid artery
fields.Venous drainage: Superior thyroid vein, middle thyroid vein, inferior thyroid vein
fields.Innervation: Middle cervical ganglion, inferior cervical ganglion
fields.Lymphatic drainage: Pretracheal, prelaryngeal, jugulodigastric lymph nodes

Superior parathyroid gland.summary: Parathyroid glands are small endocrine glands in the neck of humans and other tetrapods. Humans usually have four parathyroid glands, located on the back of the thyroid gland in variable locations. The parathyroid gland produces and secretes parathyroid hormone in response to low blood calcium, which plays a key role in regulating the amount of calcium in the blood and within the bones.

Superior parietal lobule.title: Superior parietal lobule
Superior parietal lobule.summary: The superior parietal lobule is bounded in front by the upper part of the postcentral sulcus, but is usually connected with the postcentral gyrus above the end of the sulcus. The superior parietal lobule contains Brodmann's areas 5 and 7. Behind it is the lateral part of the parieto-occipital sulcus, around the end of which it is joined to the occipital lobe by a curved gyrus, the arcus parietooccipitalis.

Superior petrosal sinus.title: Superior petrosal sinus
Superior petrosal sinus.summary: The superior petrosal sinus is one of the dural venous sinuses located beneath the brain. It receives blood from the cavernous sinus and passes backward and laterally to drain into the transverse sinus. The sinus receives superior petrosal veins, some cerebellar veins, some inferior cerebral veins, and veins from the tympanic cavity.

Superior pharyngeal constrictor.title: Superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle

fields.Origin: Medial pterygoid plate, pterygomandibular raphé, alveolar process
fields.Insertion: Pharyngeal raphe, pharyngeal tubercle
fields.Blood supply: Ascending pharyngeal artery and tonsillar branch of facial artery
fields.Action: Swallowing

Superior pharyngeal constrictor.summary: The superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle is a quadrilateral muscle of the pharynx. It is the uppermost and thinnest of the three pharyngeal constrictors. The muscle is divided into four parts according to its four distinct origins: a pterygopharyngeal, buccopharyngeal, mylopharyngeal, and a glossopharyngeal part.

Superior phrenic arteries.title: Superior phrenic arteries
Superior phrenic arteries.summary: The superior phrenic artery is a bilaterally paired artery of the thoracic cavity. The two arteries provide arterial supply to the superior surface of the diaphragm. Each artery typically arises from either (the inferior portion of) the descending part of the thoracic aorta or the 10th intercostal artery.

Superior phrenic vein.title: Superior phrenic vein
Superior phrenic vein.summary: The superior phrenic vein, i.e., the vein accompanying the pericardiacophrenic artery, usually opens into the azygos vein.

Superior pubic ligament.title: Pubic symphysis
Superior pubic ligament.summary: The pubic symphysis (pl.: symphyses) is a secondary cartilaginous joint between the left and right superior rami of the pubis of the hip bones. It is in front of and below the urinary bladder. In males, the suspensory ligament of the penis attaches to the pubic symphysis.

Superior pulmonary vein.title: Pulmonary vein
Superior pulmonary vein.summary: The pulmonary veins are the veins that transfer oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart. The largest pulmonary veins are the four main pulmonary veins, two from each lung that drain into the left atrium of the heart. The pulmonary veins are part of the pulmonary circulation.

Superior rectal artery.title: Superior rectal artery

fields.Latin: arteria rectalis superior, ; arteria haemorrhoidalis superior

Superior rectal artery.summary: The superior rectal artery (superior hemorrhoidal artery) is an artery that descends into the pelvis to supply blood to the rectum.

Superior rectal vein.title: Superior rectal vein
Superior rectal vein.summary: The inferior mesenteric vein begins in the rectum as the superior rectal vein (superior hemorrhoidal vein), which has its origin in the hemorrhoidal plexus, and through this plexus communicates with the middle and inferior hemorrhoidal veins. The superior rectal vein leaves the lesser pelvis and crosses the left common iliac vessels with the superior rectal artery, and is continued upward as the inferior mesenteric vein.

Superior rectus muscle.title: Superior rectus muscle

fields.Origin: Annulus of Zinn at the orbital apex
fields.Insertion: 7.9 mm superior to the corneal limbus
fields.Action: Elevation, adduction, intorsion

Superior rectus muscle.summary: The superior rectus muscle is one of the extraocular muscles located in the orbit. It is innervated by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve (III). In the primary position (looking straight ahead), its primary function is elevation, although it also contributes to intorsion and adduction.

Superior sagittal sinus.title: Superior sagittal sinus
Superior sagittal sinus.summary: The superior sagittal sinus (also known as the superior longitudinal sinus), within the human head, is an unpaired dural venous sinus lying along the attached margin of the falx cerebri. It allows blood to drain from the lateral aspects of the anterior cerebral hemispheres to the confluence of sinuses. Cerebrospinal fluid drains through arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus and is returned to the venous circulation.

Superior salivatory nucleus.title: Salivatory nuclei
Superior salivatory nucleus.summary: The salivatory nuclei are two general visceral efferent nuclei located in the caudal pons, dorsal and lateral to the facial nucleus. Their neurons give rise to preganglionic parasympathetic nerve fibers in the control of salivation. The superior salivatory nucleus supplies fibers to the intermediate nerve (part of the facial nerve (CN VII).

Tail of pancreas.title: Pancreas

fields.Blood supply: Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, splenic artery
fields.Innervation: Pancreatic plexus, celiac ganglia, vagus nerve
fields.Lymphatic drainage: Splenic lymph nodes, celiac lymph nodes and superior mesenteric lymph nodes

Tail of pancreas.summary: The pancreas (plural pancreases, or pancreata) is an organ of the digestive system and endocrine system of vertebrates. In humans, it is located in the abdomen behind the stomach and functions as a gland. The pancreas is a mixed or heterocrine gland, i.e., it has both an endocrine and a digestive exocrine function.

Talonavicular ligament.title: Dorsal talonavicular ligament
Talonavicular ligament.summary: The dorsal talonavicular ligament is a broad, thin band, which connects the neck of the talus to the dorsal surface of the navicular bone; it is covered by the Extensor tendons. The plantar calcaneonavicular supplies the place of a plantar ligament for this joint.

Temporal bone.title: Temporal bone

fields.Articulations: Occipital, parietal, sphenoid, mandible and zygomatic

Temporal bone.summary: The temporal bone is a paired bone situated at the sides and base of the skull, lateral to the temporal lobe of the cerebral cortex. The temporal bones are overlaid by the sides of the head known as the temples where four of the cranial bones fuse. Each temple is covered by a temporal muscle.

Temporal pole.title: Brodmann area 38
Temporal pole.summary: Brodmann area 38, also BA38 or temporopolar area 38 (H), is part of the temporal cortex in the human brain. BA 38 is at the anterior end of the temporal lobe, known as the temporal pole. BA38 is a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined temporal region of cerebral cortex.

Temporalis muscle.title: Temporalis muscle

fields.Origin: Temporal lines on the parietal bone of the skull and the superior temporal surface of the sphenoid bone
fields.Insertion: Coronoid process of the mandible and retromolar fossa
fields.Innervation: Deep temporal nerves, branches of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3)
fields.Action: Elevation and retraction of mandible

Temporalis muscle.summary: In anatomy, the temporalis muscle, also known as the temporal muscle, is one of the muscles of mastication (chewing). It is a broad, fan-shaped convergent muscle on each side of the head that fills the temporal fossa, superior to the zygomatic arch so it covers much of the temporal bone. Temporal refers to the head's temples.

Temporoparietalis muscle.title: Temporoparietalis muscle

fields.Origin: Auriculares muscles
fields.Insertion: Galea aponeurotica
fields.Innervation: Temporal branches of the facial nerve

Temporoparietalis muscle.summary: The temporoparietalis muscle is a distinct muscle of the head. It lies above the auricularis superior muscle. It lies just inferior to the epicranial aponeurosis of the occipitofrontalis muscle.

Tendinous arch of levator ani.title: Levator ani

fields.Origin: Inner surface of the side of the lesser pelvis
fields.Insertion: Inner surface of coccyx, levator ani of opposite side, and into structures that penetrate it.
fields.Innervation: S2 Pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus: *levator ani nerve (S4) *inferior rectal nerve from pudendal nerve (S3, S4) *coccygeal plexus Puborectalis: *S3, S4 *levator ani nerve
fields.Action: Supports the viscera in pelvic cavity

Tendinous arch of levator ani.summary: The levator ani is a broad, thin muscle group, situated on either side of the pelvis. It is formed from three muscle components: the puborectalis, pubococcygeus, and the iliococcygeus. It is attached to the inner surface of each side of the lesser pelvis, and these unite to form the greater part of the pelvic floor.

Tensor fasciae latae.title: Tensor fasciae latae muscle

fields.Origin: Iliac crest
fields.Insertion: Iliotibial tract (via greater trochanter)
fields.Blood supply: Primarily lateral circumflex femoral artery, superior gluteal artery
fields.Action: Hip - flexion, medial rotation, abduction, knee - lateral rotation, torso - stabilization

Tensor fasciae latae.summary: The tensor fasciae latae (or tensor fasciæ latæ or, formerly, tensor vaginae femoris) is a muscle of the thigh. Together with the gluteus maximus, it acts on and is continuous with the iliotibial band, which attaches to the tibia. The muscle assists in keeping the balance of the pelvis while standing, walking, or running.

Tensor veli palatini.title: Tensor veli palatini muscle

fields.Origin: Medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone (scaphoid fossa)
fields.Insertion: Palatine aponeurosis
fields.Action: Tension of the soft palate

Tensor veli palatini.summary: The tensor veli palatini muscle (tensor palati or tensor muscle of the velum palatinum) is a thin, triangular muscle of the head that tenses the soft palate and opens the Eustachian tube to equalise pressure in the middle ear.

Tenth rib.title: Rib cage
Tenth rib.summary: The rib cage or thoracic cage is an endoskeletal enclosure in the thorax of most vertebrates that comprises the ribs, vertebral column and sternum, which protect the vital organs of the thoracic cavity, such as the heart, lungs and great vessels and support the shoulder girdle to form the core part of the axial skeleton. A typical human thoracic cage consists of 12 pairs of ribs and the adjoining costal cartilages, the sternum (along with the manubrium and xiphoid process), and the 12 thoracic vertebrae articulating with the ribs. The thoracic cage also provides attachments for extrinsic skeletal muscles of the neck, upper limbs, upper abdomen and back, and together with the overlying skin a

Tentorium cerebelli.title: Cerebellar tentorium
Tentorium cerebelli.summary: The cerebellar tentorium or tentorium cerebelli (Latin for "tent of the cerebellum") is one of four dural folds that separate the cranial cavity into four (incomplete) compartments. The cerebellar tentorium separates the cerebellum from the cerebrum forming a supratentorial and an infratentorial region; the cerebrum is supratentorial and the cerebellum infratentorial. The free border of the tentorium gives passage to the midbrain (the upper-most part of the brainstem).

Teres major.title: Teres major muscle

fields.Origin: Posterior aspect of the inferior angle of the scapula
fields.Insertion: Medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
fields.Action: Adduct the humerus, internal rotation (medial rotation) of the humerus, extend the humerus from flexed position
fields.Innervation: Lower subscapular nerve (segmental levels C5 and C6)

Teres major.summary: The teres major muscle is a muscle of the upper limb. It attaches to the scapula and the humerus and is one of the seven scapulohumeral muscles. It is a thick but somewhat flattened muscle.

Teres major muscle.title: Teres major muscle

fields.Origin: Posterior aspect of the inferior angle of the scapula
fields.Insertion: Medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
fields.Action: Adduct the humerus, internal rotation (medial rotation) of the humerus, extend the humerus from flexed position
fields.Innervation: Lower subscapular nerve (segmental levels C5 and C6)

Teres major muscle.summary: The teres major muscle is a muscle of the upper limb. It attaches to the scapula and the humerus and is one of the seven scapulohumeral muscles. It is a thick but somewhat flattened muscle.

Teres minor.title: Teres minor muscle

fields.Origin: Lateral border of the scapula
fields.Insertion: Inferior facet of greater tubercle of the humerus
fields.Blood supply: Posterior circumflex humeral artery and the circumflex scapular artery
fields.Action: Laterally rotates the arm, stabilizes humerus

Teres minor.summary: The teres minor (Latin teres meaning 'rounded') is a narrow, elongated muscle of the rotator cuff. The muscle originates from the lateral border and adjacent posterior surface of the corresponding right or left scapula and inserts at both the greater tubercle of the humerus and the posterior surface of the joint capsule. The primary function of the teres minor is to modulate the action of the deltoid, preventing the humeral head from sliding upward as the arm is abducted.

Teres minor muscle.title: Teres minor muscle

fields.Origin: Lateral border of the scapula
fields.Insertion: Inferior facet of greater tubercle of the humerus
fields.Blood supply: Posterior circumflex humeral artery and the circumflex scapular artery
fields.Action: Laterally rotates the arm, stabilizes humerus

Teres minor muscle.summary: The teres minor (Latin teres meaning 'rounded') is a narrow, elongated muscle of the rotator cuff. The muscle originates from the lateral border and adjacent posterior surface of the corresponding right or left scapula and inserts at both the greater tubercle of the humerus and the posterior surface of the joint capsule. The primary function of the teres minor is to modulate the action of the deltoid, preventing the humeral head from sliding upward as the arm is abducted.

Testicular artery.title: Testicular artery
Testicular artery.summary: The testicular artery (the male gonadal artery, also called the internal spermatic arteries in older texts) is a branch of the abdominal aorta that supplies blood to the testicle. It is a paired artery, with one for each of the testicles. It is the male equivalent of the ovarian artery.

Testicular vein.title: Testicular vein

fields.Drains to: Inferior vena cava, left renal vein

Testicular vein.summary: The testicular vein (or spermatic vein), the male gonadal vein, carries deoxygenated blood from its corresponding testis to the inferior vena cava or one of its tributaries. It is the male equivalent of the ovarian vein, and is the venous counterpart of the testicular artery.

Testis.title: Testicle

fields.Lymphatic drainage: Lumbar lymph nodes

Testis.summary: A testicle, also called testis (pl. testes) is the male gonad in all gonochoric animals, including humans, and is homologous to the ovary, which is the female gonad. Its primary functions are the production of sperm and the secretion of androgens, primarily testosterone.

Thalamogeniculate artery.title: Thalamogeniculate artery
Thalamogeniculate artery.summary: The thalamogeniculate artery is either a single artery or group of smaller arteries arising from the posterior cerebral artery (distal to the origin of the posterior communicating artery). It is part of the posterolateral central arteries. It supplies parts of the thalamus (including the geniculate nuclei).

Thalamoperforating artery.title: Central arteries
Thalamoperforating artery.summary: Central arteries (or perforating or ganglionic arteries) of the brain are numerous small arteries branching from the Circle of Willis, and adjacent arteries that often enter the substance of the brain through the anterior and posterior perforated substances. They supply structures of the base of the brain and internal structures of the cerebral hemispheres. They are separated into four principal groups: anteromedial central arteries; anterolateral central arteries (lenticulostriate arteries); posteromedial central arteries (paramedian arteries); and posterolateral central arteries.

Thalamus.title: Thalamus
Thalamus.summary: The thalamus (pl.: thalami; from Greek θάλαμος, "chamber") is a large mass of gray matter on the lateral wall of the third ventricle forming the dorsal part of the diencephalon (a division of the forebrain). Nerve fibers project out of the thalamus to the cerebral cortex in all directions, known as the thalamocortical radiations, allowing hub-like exchanges of information. It has several functions, such as the relaying of sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex and the regulation of consciousness, sleep, and alertness.

Third metacarpal bone.title: Third metacarpal bone
Third metacarpal bone.summary: The third metacarpal bone (metacarpal bone of the middle finger) is a little smaller than the second. The dorsal aspect of its base presents on its radial side a pyramidal eminence, the styloid process, which extends upward behind the capitate; immediately distal to this is a rough surface for the attachment of the extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle. The carpal articular facet is concave behind, flat in front, and articulates with the capitate.

Third metatarsal bone.title: Third metatarsal bone
Third metatarsal bone.summary: The third metatarsal bone is a long bone in the foot. It is the second longest metatarsal, the longest being the second metatarsal. The third metatarsal is analogous to the third metacarpal bone in the hand Like the four other metatarsal bones, it can be divided into three part: base, body and head.

Third rib.title: Rib cage
Third rib.summary: The rib cage or thoracic cage is an endoskeletal enclosure in the thorax of most vertebrates that comprises the ribs, vertebral column and sternum, which protect the vital organs of the thoracic cavity, such as the heart, lungs and great vessels and support the shoulder girdle to form the core part of the axial skeleton. A typical human thoracic cage consists of 12 pairs of ribs and the adjoining costal cartilages, the sternum (along with the manubrium and xiphoid process), and the 12 thoracic vertebrae articulating with the ribs. The thoracic cage also provides attachments for extrinsic skeletal muscles of the neck, upper limbs, upper abdomen and back, and together with the overlying skin a

Third ventricle.title: Third ventricle
Third ventricle.summary: The third ventricle is one of the four connected cerebral ventricles of the ventricular system within the mammalian brain. It is a slit-like cavity formed in the diencephalon between the two thalami, in the midline between the right and left lateral ventricles, and is filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Running through the third ventricle is the interthalamic adhesion, which contains thalamic neurons and fibers that may connect the two thalami.

Thoracic aorta.title: Thoracic aorta

fields.Branches: Bronchial arteries, esophageal arteries, posterior intercostal arteries, abdominal aorta, superior phrenic artery, pericardial arteries

Thoracic aorta.summary: The thoracic aorta is a part of the aorta located in the thorax. It is a continuation of the aortic arch. It is located within the posterior mediastinal cavity, but frequently bulges into the left pleural cavity.

Thoracic vertebra 1.title: Thoracic vertebrae
Thoracic vertebra 1.summary: In vertebrates, thoracic vertebrae compose the middle segment of the vertebral column, between the cervical vertebrae and the lumbar vertebrae. In humans, there are twelve thoracic vertebrae of intermediate size between the cervical and lumbar vertebrae; they increase in size going towards the lumbar vertebrae. They are distinguished by the presence of facets on the sides of the bodies for articulation with the heads of the ribs, as well as facets on the transverse processes of all, except the eleventh and twelfth, for articulation with the tubercles of the ribs.

Thoracic vertebra 10.title: Thoracic vertebrae
Thoracic vertebra 10.summary: In vertebrates, thoracic vertebrae compose the middle segment of the vertebral column, between the cervical vertebrae and the lumbar vertebrae. Thoraco-acromial artery.title: Thoracoacromial artery
Thoraco-acromial artery.summary: The thoracoacromial artery (acromiothoracic artery; thoracic axis) is a short trunk that arises from the second part of the axillary artery, its origin being generally overlapped by the upper edge of the pectoralis minor.

Thoracodorsal artery.title: Thoracodorsal artery
Thoracodorsal artery.summary: The thoracodorsal artery is a branch of the subscapular artery. It passes inferior-ward upon the surface of the serratus anterior muscle (which it supplies posteroinferiorly to the lateral thoracic artery). It is accompanied by the thoracodorsal nerve along its source.

Thoracodorsal nerve.title: Thoracodorsal nerve
Thoracodorsal nerve.summary: The thoracodorsal nerve is a nerve present in humans and other animals, also known as the middle subscapular nerve or the long subscapular nerve. It supplies the latissimus dorsi muscle.

Thyro-arytenoid.title: Thyroarytenoid muscle

fields.Origin: Inner surface of the thyroid cartilage (anterior aspect)
fields.Insertion: Anterior surface of arytenoid cartilage
fields.Innervation: Recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus
fields.Action: Helps to reduce tension on the vocal folds during speech to decrease pitch

Thyro-arytenoid.summary: The thyroarytenoid muscle is a broad, thin muscle that forms the body of the vocal fold and that supports the wall of the ventricle and its appendix. It functions to shorten the vocal folds.

Thyrocervical trunk.title: Thyrocervical trunk

fields.Branches: Inferior thyroid artery; Suprascapular artery; Transverse cervical artery

Thyrocervical trunk.summary: The thyrocervical trunks are very small arteries of the neck arising from the subclavian arteries, lateral to the vertebral arteries. They divide into branches: the inferior thyroid artery, suprascapular artery, and the transverse cervical artery. The thyrocervical trunks supply the thyroid gland and some scapular muscles.

Thyrohyoid.title: Thyrohyoid muscle

fields.Origin: Thyroid cartilage of the larynx
fields.Insertion: Hyoid bone
fields.Action: Elevates thyroid and depresses the hyoid bone
fields.Innervation: First cervical nerve (C1) via hypoglossal nerve

Thyrohyoid.summary: The thyrohyoid muscle is a small skeletal muscle of the neck. Above, it attaches onto the greater cornu of the hyoid bone; below, it attaches onto the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage. It is innervated by fibres derived from the cervical spinal nerve 1 that run with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) to reach this muscle.

Thyrohyoid membrane.title: Thyrohyoid membrane
Thyrohyoid membrane.summary: The thyrohyoid membrane (or hyothyroid membrane) is a broad, fibro-elastic sheet of the larynx. It connects the upper border of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone.

Thyrohyoid muscle.title: Thyrohyoid muscle

fields.Origin: Thyroid cartilage of the larynx
fields.Insertion: Hyoid bone
fields.Action: Elevates thyroid and depresses the hyoid bone
fields.Innervation: First cervical nerve (C1) via hypoglossal nerve

Thyrohyoid muscle.summary: The thyrohyoid muscle is a small skeletal muscle of the neck. Above, it attaches onto the greater cornu of the hyoid bone; below, it attaches onto the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage. It is innervated by fibres derived from the cervical spinal nerve 1 that run with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) to reach this muscle.

Thyroid cartilage.title: Thyroid cartilage
Thyroid cartilage.summary: The thyroid cartilage is the largest of the nine cartilages that make up the laryngeal skeleton, the cartilage structure in and around the trachea that contains the larynx. It does not completely encircle the larynx (only the cricoid cartilage encircles it).

Thyroid gland.title: Thyroid

fields.Develops from: Thyroid diverticulum (an extension of endoderm into 2nd pharyngeal arch)

Thyroid gland.summary: The thyroid, or thyroid gland, is an endocrine gland in vertebrates. In humans, it is a butterfly-shaped or H-shaped gland located in the neck below the Adam's apple. It consists of two connected lobes.

Tibia.title: Tibia

fields.Articulations: Knee, ankle, superior and ; inferior tibiofibular joint

Tibia.summary: The tibia (; pl.: tibiae or tibias), also known as the shinbone, shankbone or simply the shin, is the larger, stronger, and anterior (frontal) of the two bones in the leg below the knee in vertebrates (the other being the fibula, behind and to the outside of the tibia); it connects the knee with the ankle. The tibia is found on the medial side of the leg next to the fibula and closer to the median plane. The tibia is connected to the fibula by the interosseous membrane of leg, forming a type of fibrous joint called a syndesmosis with very little movement.

Tibial collateral ligament.title: Medial collateral ligament
Tibial collateral ligament.summary: The medial collateral ligament (MCL), also called the superficial medial collateral ligament (sMCL) or tibial collateral ligament (TCL), is one of the major ligaments of the knee. It is on the medial (inner) side of the knee joint and occurs in humans and other primates. Its primary function is to resist valgus (inward bending) forces on the knee.

Tibial nerve.title: Tibial nerve

fields.Innervates: Origin: Flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus; Anterior: semimembranosus, semitendinosus, long head of biceps femoris ; Medial: abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis, first lumbrical; Lateral: quadratus plantae, flexor digiti minimi, adductor hallucis, the interossei, three lumbricals and abductor digiti minimi
fields.Branches: Medial plantar nerve, lateral plantar nerve

Tibial nerve.summary: The tibial nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve. The tibial nerve passes through the popliteal fossa to pass below the arch of soleus.

Tibialis anterior.title: Tibialis anterior muscle

fields.Origin: From the upper 1/2 or 2/3 of the lateral surface of the tibia and the adjacent interosseous membrane
fields.Insertion: Medial cuneiform and the base of first metatarsal bone of the foot
fields.Action: Dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot
fields.Antagonist: Fibularis longus, gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, tibialis posterior

Tibialis anterior.summary: The tibialis anterior muscle is a muscle of the anterior compartment of the lower leg. It originates from the upper portion of the tibia; it inserts into the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal bones of the foot. It acts to dorsiflex and invert the foot.

Tibialis anterior muscle.title: Tibialis anterior muscle

fields.Origin: From the upper 1/2 or 2/3 of the lateral surface of the tibia and the adjacent interosseous membrane
fields.Insertion: Medial cuneiform and the base of first metatarsal bone of the foot
fields.Action: Dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot
fields.Antagonist: Fibularis longus, gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, tibialis posterior

Tibialis anterior muscle.summary: The tibialis anterior muscle is a muscle of the anterior compartment of the lower leg. It originates from the upper portion of the tibia; it inserts into the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal bones of the foot. It acts to dorsiflex and invert the foot.

Tibialis posterior.title: Tibialis posterior muscle

fields.Origin: Tibia and fibula
fields.Insertion: Navicular and medial cuneiform bone
fields.Action: Inversion of the foot and plantar flexion of the foot at the ankle
fields.Antagonist: Fibularis brevis and longus, antagonist to the inversion

Tibialis posterior.summary: The tibialis posterior muscle is the most central of all the leg muscles, and is located in the deep posterior compartment of the leg. It is the key stabilizing muscle of the lower leg.

Tibialis posterior muscle.title: Tibialis posterior muscle

fields.Origin: Tibia and fibula
fields.Insertion: Navicular and medial cuneiform bone
fields.Action: Inversion of the foot and plantar flexion of the foot at the ankle
fields.Antagonist: Fibularis brevis and longus, antagonist to the inversion

Tibialis posterior muscle.summary: The tibialis posterior muscle is the most central of all the leg muscles, and is located in the deep posterior compartment of the leg. It is the key stabilizing muscle of the lower leg.

Tongue.title: Tongue

fields.Develops from: Pharyngeal arches, lateral lingual swelling, tuberculum impar
fields.Innervation: Sensory; Anterior two-thirds: Lingual (sensation) and chorda tympani (taste); Posterior one-third: Glossopharyngeal (IX); Motor; Hypoglossal (XII), except palatoglossus muscle supplied by the pharyngeal plexus via vagus (X)
fields.Lymphatic drainage: Deep cervical, submandibular, submental

Tongue.summary: The tongue is a muscular organ in the mouth of a typical tetrapod. It manipulates food for chewing and swallowing as part of the digestive process and is the primary organ of taste. The tongue's upper surface (dorsum) is covered by taste buds housed in numerous lingual papillae.

Tonsil of cerebellum.title: Cerebellar tonsil
Tonsil of cerebellum.summary: The cerebellar tonsil (Latin: tonsilla cerebelli) is a paired rounded lobule on the undersurface of each cerebellar hemisphere, continuous medially with the uvula of the cerebellar vermis and superiorly by the flocculonodular lobe. Synonyms include: tonsilla cerebelli, amygdala cerebelli, the latter of which is not to be confused with the cerebral tonsils or amygdala nuclei located deep within the medial temporal lobes of the cerebral cortex. The flocculonodular lobe of the cerebellum, which can also be confused for the cerebellar tonsils, is one of three lobes that make up the overall composition of the cerebellum.

Trabecular meshwork.title: Trabecular meshwork
Trabecular meshwork.summary: The trabecular meshwork is an area of tissue in the eye located around the base of the cornea, near the ciliary body, and is responsible for draining the aqueous humor from the eye via the anterior chamber (the chamber on the front of the eye covered by the cornea). The tissue is spongy and lined by trabeculocytes; it allows fluid to drain into a set of tubes called Schlemm's canal which is lined by endothelium with blood and lymphatic properties that allow aqueous humor to flow into the blood system.

Trachea.title: Trachea

fields.Blood supply: Tracheal branches of inferior thyroid artery
fields.Venous drainage: Brachiocephalic vein, azygos vein, accessory hemiazygos vein

Trachea.summary: The trachea (pl.: tracheae or tracheas), also known as the windpipe, is a cartilaginous tube that connects the larynx to the bronchi of the lungs, allowing the passage of air, and so is present in almost all land vertebrate animals' lungs. The trachea extends from the larynx and branches into the two primary bronchi. At the top of the trachea, the cricoid cartilage attaches it to the larynx.

Tracheal cartilage.title: Trachea

fields.Blood supply: Tracheal branches of inferior thyroid artery
fields.Venous drainage: Brachiocephalic vein, azygos vein, accessory hemiazygos vein

Tracheal cartilage.summary: The trachea (pl.: tracheae or tracheas), also known as the windpipe, is a cartilaginous tube that connects the larynx to the bronchi of the lungs, allowing the passage of air, and so is present in almost all land vertebrate animals' lungs. The trachea extends from the larynx and branches into the two primary bronchi. At the top of the trachea, the cricoid cartilage attaches it to the larynx.

Transversalis fascia.title: Transversalis fascia
Transversalis fascia.summary: The transversalis fascia (also Hyrtl fascia or transverse fascia) is the fascial lining of the anterolateral abdominal wall situated between the inner surface of the transverse abdominal muscle, and the preperitoneal fascia. It is directly continuous with the iliac fascia, the internal spermatic fascia, and pelvic fascia.

Transverse acetabular ligament.title: Transverse acetabular ligament
Transverse acetabular ligament.summary: The transverse acetabular ligament (transverse ligament or Tunstall's ligament) bridges the acetabular notch, creating the a foramen (through which blood vessels and nerves pass into the joint cavity). The ligament is one of the sites of attachment of the ligament of head of femur. Some sources consider the transverse acetabular ligament as the part of the acetabular labrum over the acetabular notch, while another states that the labrum attaches onto the ligament.

Transverse arytenoid.title: Transverse arytenoid
Transverse arytenoid.summary: The transverse arytenoid is an unpaired intrinsic muscle of the larynx. It is situated deep to the two oblique arytenoids; the oblique and transverse arytenoids are often considered two parts of a single muscle - the interarytenoid (arytenoid) muscle (which is then said to have an oblique part and a transverse part). The transverse arytenoid bridges the gap between the two arytenoid cartilage in the larynx, occupying the concavity of the lateral surface of each cartilage.

Transverse arytenoid muscle.title: Arytenoid muscle

fields.Origin: Arytenoid cartilage on one side
fields.Insertion: Arytenoid cartilage on opposite side
fields.Innervation: Recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus
fields.Action: Approximate the arytenoid cartilages (close rima glottis)

Transverse arytenoid muscle.summary: The arytenoid muscle or interarytenoid muscle is a composite intrinsic muscle of the larynx, consisting of a transverse part and an oblique part - the two parts may be considered as separate muscles: an unpaired transverse arytenoid muscle, and a bilaterally paired oblique arytenoid muscle. The two constituent parts differ in their attachments, structure and actions. Both receive motor innervation from the recurrent laryngeal nerve(s) (each nerve being a branch of one vagus nerve (CN X)).

Transverse cervical artery.title: Transverse cervical artery

fields.Latin: arteria transversa cervicis, ; arteria transversa colli
fields.Branches: Superficial branch ; dorsal scapular artery (deep branch)

Transverse cervical artery.summary: The transverse cervical artery (transverse artery of neck or transversa colli artery) is an artery in the neck and a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, running at a higher level than the suprascapular artery.

Transverse colon.title: Transverse colon
Transverse colon.summary: In human anatomy, the transverse colon is the longest and most movable part of the colon.

Transverse facial artery.title: Transverse facial artery

fields.Supplies: Parotid gland; parotid duct ; masseter muscle

Transverse facial artery.summary: The transverse facial artery is an artery that branches from the superficial temporal artery and runs across the face.

Transverse humeral ligament.title: Transverse humeral ligament
Transverse humeral ligament.summary: The transverse humeral ligament (Brodie's ligament) forms a broad band bridging the lesser and greater tubercle of the humerus. Its attachments are limited superior to the epiphysial line. By enclosing the canal of the bicipital groove (intertubercular groove), it functions to hold the long head of the biceps tendon within the bicipital groove.

Transverse intermuscular septum of leg.title: Deep transverse fascia
Transverse intermuscular septum of leg.summary: The deep transverse fascia or transverse intermuscular septum of leg is a transversely placed, intermuscular septum, from the deep fascia, between the superficial and deep muscles of the back of the leg. At the sides it is connected to the margins of the tibia and fibula. Above, where it covers the popliteus, it is thick and dense, and receives an expansion from the tendon of the semimembranosus.

Transverse ligament of knee.title: Transverse ligament of knee
Transverse ligament of knee.summary: The transverse or (anterior) meniscomeniscal ligament is a ligament in the knee joint that connects the anterior convex margin of the lateral meniscus to the anterior end of the medial meniscus. It is divided into several strips in ten percent of subjects and its thickness varies considerably in different subjects.

Transverse occipital sulcus.title: Transverse occipital sulcus
Transverse occipital sulcus.summary: The transverse occipital sulcus is a sulcus in the occipital lobe. The transverse occipital sulcus is continuous with the posterior end of the occipital ramus of the intraparietal sulcus, and runs across the upper part of the lobe, a short distance behind the parietooccipital fissure.

Transverse sinus.title: Transverse sinuses

fields.Source: Confluence of sinuses, superior sagittal sinus

Transverse sinus.summary: The transverse sinuses (left and right lateral sinuses), within the human head, are two areas beneath the brain which allow blood to drain from the back of the head. They run laterally in a groove along the interior surface of the occipital bone. They drain from the confluence of sinuses (by the internal occipital protuberance) to the sigmoid sinuses, which ultimately connect to the internal jugular vein.

Transverse temporal gyri.title: Transverse temporal gyrus
Transverse temporal gyri.summary: The transverse temporal gyrus, also called Heschl's gyrus () or Heschl's convolutions, is a gyrus found in the area of each primary auditory cortex buried within the lateral sulcus of the human brain, occupying Brodmann areas 41 and 42. Transverse temporal gyri are superior to and separated from the planum temporale (cortex involved in language production) by Heschl's sulcus. Transverse temporal gyri are found in varying numbers in both the right and left hemispheres of the brain and one study found that this number is not related to the hemisphere or dominance of hemisphere studied in subjects.

Transversus abdominis muscle.title: Transverse abdominal muscle

fields.Origin: Iliac crest, inguinal ligament, thoracolumbar fascia, and costal cartilages 7-12
fields.Insertion: Xiphoid process, linea alba, pubic crest and pecten pubis via conjoint tendon
fields.Innervation: Thoracoabdominal nn. (T6-T11), Subcostal n. (T12), iliohypogastric nerve (L1), and ilioinguinal nerve (L1)
fields.Action: Compresses abdominal contents (bilateral), rotates trunk ipsilaterally (unilateral)

Transversus abdominis muscle.summary: The transverse abdominal muscle (TVA), also known as the transverse abdominis, transversalis muscle and transversus abdominis muscle, is a muscle layer of the anterior and lateral (front and side) abdominal wall, deep to (layered below) the internal oblique muscle. It serves to compress and retain the contents of the abdomen as well as assist in exhalation.

Transversus thoracis.title: Transversus thoracis muscle

fields.Origin: Costal cartilages of last 3-4 true ribs, body of sternum and xiphoid process
fields.Insertion: Ribs/costal cartilages 2-6
fields.Action: Depresses ribs

Transversus thoracis.summary: The transversus thoracis muscle (), also known as triangularis sterni, lies internal to the thoracic cage, anteriorly. It is usually a thin plane of muscular and tendinous fibers, however on athletic individuals it can be a thick 'slab of meat', situated upon the inner surface of the front wall of the chest. It is in the same layer as the subcostal muscles and the innermost intercostal muscles.

Transversus thoracis muscle.title: Transversus thoracis muscle

fields.Origin: Costal cartilages of last 3-4 true ribs, body of sternum and xiphoid process
fields.Insertion: Ribs/costal cartilages 2-6
fields.Action: Depresses ribs

Transversus thoracis muscle.summary: The transversus thoracis muscle (), also known as triangularis sterni, lies internal to the thoracic cage, anteriorly. It is usually a thin plane of muscular and tendinous fibers, however on athletic individuals it can be a thick 'slab of meat', situated upon the inner surface of the front wall of the chest. It is in the same layer as the subcostal muscles and the innermost intercostal muscles.

Trapezium.title: Trapezium
Trapezium.summary: Trapezium, plural trapeziums or trapezia, may refer to:

Trapezium bone.title: Trapezium (bone)

fields.Articulations: 1st metacarpal distally ; scaphoid proximally ; trapezoid medially ; 2nd metacarpal medially

Trapezium bone.summary: The trapezium bone (greater multangular bone) is a carpal bone in the hand. It forms the radial border of the carpal tunnel.

Trapezoid bone.title: Trapezoid bone

fields.Articulations: Articulates with four bones:; scaphoid proximally; second metacarpal distally; trapezium bone laterally; capitate medially

Trapezoid bone.summary: The trapezoid bone (lesser multangular bone) is a carpal bone in tetrapods, including humans. It is the smallest bone in the distal row of carpal bones that give structure to the palm of the hand. It may be known by its wedge-shaped form, the broad end of the wedge constituting the dorsal, the narrow end the palmar surface; and by its having four articular facets touching each other, and separated by sharp edges.

Trapezoid ligament.title: Trapezoid ligament
Trapezoid ligament.summary: The trapezoid ligament is a ligament connecting the coracoid process of the scapula (the shoulder blade) to the trapezoid line of the clavicle (collarbone). It is an anterior and lateral fasciculus, and is broad, thin, and quadrilateral. Its anterior border is free; its posterior border is joined with the conoid ligament, the two forming, by their junction, an angle projecting backward.

Triangular part of inferior frontal gyru.title: Inferior frontal gyrus
Triangular part of inferior frontal gyru.summary: The inferior frontal gyrus (IFG; also gyrus frontalis inferior) is the lowest positioned gyrus of the frontal gyri, of the frontal lobe, and is part of the prefrontal cortex. Its superior border is the inferior frontal sulcus (which divides it from the middle frontal gyrus), its inferior border is the lateral sulcus (which divides it from the superior temporal gyrus) and its posterior border is the inferior precentral sulcus. Above it is the middle frontal gyrus, behind it is the precentral gyrus.

Tricuspid valve.title: Tricuspid valve
Tricuspid valve.summary: The tricuspid valve, or right atrioventricular valve, is on the right dorsal side of the mammalian heart, at the superior portion of the right ventricle. The function of the valve is to allow blood to flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle during diastole, and to close to prevent backflow (regurgitation) from the right ventricle into the right atrium during right ventricular contraction (systole).

Trigone of urinary bladder.title: Trigone of urinary bladder
Trigone of urinary bladder.summary: The trigone of urinary bladder (also known as the vesical trigone) is a smooth triangular region of the urinary bladder formed by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. Between the ureteric openings, there is a fold of mucous membrane called the interureteric crest or Mercier bar. The trigone lies between the crest or ridge, and the neck of the bladder.

Triquetral.title: Triquetral bone

fields.Articulations: Articulates with three bones:; lunate laterally; pisiform in front; hamate distally; triangular articular disk which separates it from the lower end of the ulna.

Triquetral.summary: The triquetral bone (; also called triquetrum, pyramidal, three-faced, and formerly cuneiform bone) is located in the wrist on the medial side of the proximal row of the carpus between the lunate and pisiform bones. It is on the ulnar side of the hand, but does not directly articulate with the ulna. Instead, it is connected to and articulates with the ulna through the Triangular fibrocartilage disc and ligament, which forms part of the ulnocarpal joint capsule.

Triquetrum bone.title: Triquetral bone

fields.Articulations: Articulates with three bones:; lunate laterally; pisiform in front; hamate distally; triangular articular disk which separates it from the lower end of the ulna.

Triquetrum bone.summary: The triquetral bone (; also called triquetrum, pyramidal, three-faced, and formerly cuneiform bone) is located in the wrist on the medial side of the proximal row of the carpus between the lunate and pisiform bones. It is on the ulnar side of the hand, but does not directly articulate with the ulna. Instead, it is connected to and articulates with the ulna through the Triangular fibrocartilage disc and ligament, which forms part of the ulnocarpal joint capsule.

Triradiate cartilage.title: Triradiate cartilage
Triradiate cartilage.summary: The triradiate cartilage (in Latin cartilago ypsiloformis) is the Y-shaped epiphyseal plate between the ilium, ischium and pubis to form the acetabulum of the os coxae.

Trochlea of superior oblique muscle.title: Trochlea of superior oblique
Trochlea of superior oblique muscle.summary: The trochlea of superior oblique is a pulley-like structure in the eye. The tendon of the superior oblique muscle passes through it. It is the only cartilage found in the normal orbit, on the superior nasal aspect of the frontal bone.

Trochlear nerve.title: Trochlear nerve
Trochlear nerve.summary: The trochlear nerve (), (lit. pulley-like nerve) also known as the fourth cranial nerve, cranial nerve IV, or CN IV, is a cranial nerve that innervates a single muscle - the superior oblique muscle of the eye (which operates through the pulley-like trochlea). Unlike most other cranial nerves, the trochlear nerve is exclusively a motor nerve (somatic efferent nerve).

Tuber of vermis.title: Tuber of vermis
Tuber of vermis.summary: The tuber of vermis, the most posterior division of the inferior vermis, is of small size, and laterally spreads out into the large inferior semilunar lobules, which comprise at least two-thirds of the inferior surface of the hemisphere.

Twelfth rib.title: Rib cage
Twelfth rib.summary: The rib cage or thoracic cage is an endoskeletal enclosure in the thorax of most vertebrates that comprises the ribs, vertebral column and sternum, which protect the vital organs of the thoracic cavity, such as the heart, lungs and great vessels and support the shoulder girdle to form the core part of the axial skeleton. A typical human thoracic cage consists of 12 pairs of ribs and the adjoining costal cartilages, the sternum (along with the manubrium and xiphoid process), and the 12 thoracic vertebrae articulating with the ribs. The thoracic cage also provides attachments for extrinsic skeletal muscles of the neck, upper limbs, upper abdomen and back, and together with the overlying skin a

Ulna.title: Ulna
Ulna.summary: The ulna or ulnar bone (pl.: ulnae or ulnas) is a long bone in the forearm stretching from the elbow to the wrist. It is on the same side of the forearm as the little finger, running parallel to the radius, the forearm's other long bone. Longer and thinner than the radius, the ulna is considered to be the smaller long bone of the lower arm.

Ulnar artery.title: Ulnar artery

fields.Branches: Anterior ulnar recurrent artery ; posterior ulnar recurrent artery ; common interosseous artery (volar, dorsal, recurrent interosseous artery); muscular artery ; volar carpal ; dorsal carpal ; deep volar ; superficial volar arch

Ulnar artery.summary: The ulnar artery is the main blood vessel, with oxygenated blood, of the medial aspects of the forearm. It arises from the brachial artery and terminates in the superficial palmar arch, which joins with the superficial branch of the radial artery. It is palpable on the anterior and medial aspect of the wrist.

Ulnar collateral ligament.title: Ulnar collateral ligament
Ulnar collateral ligament.summary: Ulnar collateral ligament (or UCL) may refer to:

Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint.title: Ulnar carpal collateral ligament
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint.summary: The ulnar collateral ligament (internal lateral ligament, ulnar carpal collateral ligament or ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist joint) is a rounded cord, attached above to the end of the styloid process of the ulna, and dividing below into two fasciculi, one of which is attached to the medial side of the triquetral bone, the other to the pisiform and flexor retinaculum.

Ulnar nerve.title: Ulnar nerve

fields.Innervates: Flexor carpi ulnaris; flexor digitorum profundus; lumbrical muscles; opponens digiti minimi; flexor digiti minimi; abductor digiti minimi; interossei; adductor pollicis

Ulnar nerve.summary: The ulnar nerve is a nerve that runs near the ulna, one of the two long bones in the forearm. The ulnar collateral ligament of elbow joint is in relation with the ulnar nerve. The nerve is the largest in the human body unprotected by muscle or bone, so injury is common.

Ulnar recurrent artery.title: Ulnar recurrent artery
Ulnar recurrent artery.summary: Ulnar recurrent artery can refer to:

Ulnar vein.title: Ulnar veins
Ulnar vein.summary: The ulnar veins are venae comitantes of the ulnar artery. They drain the superficial venous palmar arch. They arise in the hand and terminate by uniting with the radial veins to form the brachial veins.

Ulnar veins.title: Ulnar veins
Ulnar veins.summary: The ulnar veins are venae comitantes of the ulnar artery. They drain the superficial venous palmar arch. They arise in the hand and terminate by uniting with the radial veins to form the brachial veins.

Umbilical vein.title: Umbilical vein
Umbilical vein.summary: The umbilical vein is a vein present during fetal development that carries oxygenated blood from the placenta into the growing fetus. The umbilical vein provides convenient access to the central circulation of a neonate for restoration of blood volume and for administration of glucose and drugs. The blood pressure inside the umbilical vein is approximately 20 mmHg.

Urinary bladder.title: Bladder

fields.Blood supply: Superior vesical artery; inferior vesical artery; umbilical artery; vaginal artery, internal pudendal artery, deep external pudendal artery
fields.Lymphatic drainage: Preaortic lymph nodes

Urinary bladder.summary: The bladder (from Old English blædre 'bladder, blister, pimple') is a hollow organ that stores urine from the kidneys of vertebrates. In humans and other placental mammals, urine enters the bladder via the ureters and exits via the urethra. In humans, the bladder is a distensible organ that sits on the pelvic floor.

Uterine artery.title: Uterine artery

fields.Supplies: Round ligament of the uterus, ovary, uterus, vagina, uterine tube

Uterine artery.summary: The uterine artery is an artery that supplies blood to the uterus in females.

Uterine vein.title: Uterine vein
Uterine vein.summary: The uterine vein is a vein of the uterus. It is found in the cardinal ligament. It drains into the internal iliac vein.

Uterosacral ligament.title: Uterosacral ligament
Uterosacral ligament.summary: The uterosacral ligaments (or rectouterine ligaments) are major ligaments of uterus that extend posterior-ward from the cervix to attach onto the (anterior aspect of the) sacrum.

Vagina.title: Vagina

fields.Blood supply: Superior part to uterine artery, middle and inferior parts to vaginal artery
fields.Lymphatic drainage: Upper part to internal iliac lymph nodes, lower part to superficial inguinal lymph nodes

Vagina.summary: The vagina (pl.: vaginas or vaginae) is the elastic, muscular reproductive organ of the female genital tract through which mammals copulate and give birth. In humans, it extends from the vulval vestibule to the cervix (neck of the uterus). The vaginal introitus is normally partly covered by a thin layer of mucosal tissue called the hymen.

Vastus intermedius.title: Vastus intermedius muscle

fields.Origin: Anterolateral femur
fields.Insertion: Quadriceps tendon
fields.Action: Extension of knee joint

Vastus intermedius.summary: The vastus intermedius () (Cruraeus) arises from the front and lateral surfaces of the body of the femur in its upper two-thirds, sitting under the rectus femoris muscle and from the lower part of the lateral intermuscular septum. Its fibers end in a superficial aponeurosis, which forms the deep part of the quadriceps femoris tendon. The vastus medialis and vastus intermedius appear to be inseparably united, but when the rectus femoris has been reflected during dissection a narrow interval will be observed extending upward from the medial border of the patella between the two muscles, and the separation may be continued as far as the lower part of the intertrochanteric line, where, however,

Vastus intermedius muscle.title: Vastus intermedius muscle

fields.Origin: Anterolateral femur
fields.Insertion: Quadriceps tendon
fields.Action: Extension of knee joint

Vastus intermedius muscle.summary: The vastus intermedius () (Cruraeus) arises from the front and lateral surfaces of the body of the femur in its upper two-thirds, sitting under the rectus femoris muscle and from the lower part of the lateral intermuscular septum. Its fibers end in a superficial aponeurosis, which forms the deep part of the quadriceps femoris tendon. The vastus medialis and vastus intermedius appear to be inseparably united, but when the rectus femoris has been reflected during dissection a narrow interval will be observed extending upward from the medial border of the patella between the two muscles, and the separation may be continued as far as the lower part of the intertrochanteric line, where, however,

Vastus lateralis.title: Vastus lateralis muscle

fields.Latin: musculus vastus lateralis or musculus vastus externus
fields.Origin: Greater trochanter, intertrochanteric line, and linea aspera of the femur
fields.Insertion: Patella by the quadriceps tendon and tibial tuberosity by the patellar ligament
fields.Action: Extends and stabilizes knee

Vastus lateralis.summary: The vastus lateralis (), also called the vastus externus, is the largest and most powerful part of the quadriceps femoris, a muscle in the thigh. Together with other muscles of the quadriceps group, it serves to extend the knee joint, moving the lower leg forward. It arises from a series of flat, broad tendons attached to the femur, and attaches to the outer border of the patella.

Vastus lateralis muscle.title: Vastus lateralis muscle

fields.Latin: musculus vastus lateralis or musculus vastus externus
fields.Origin: Greater trochanter, intertrochanteric line, and linea aspera of the femur
fields.Insertion: Patella by the quadriceps tendon and tibial tuberosity by the patellar ligament
fields.Action: Extends and stabilizes knee

Vastus lateralis muscle.summary: The vastus lateralis (), also called the vastus externus, is the largest and most powerful part of the quadriceps femoris, a muscle in the thigh. Together with other muscles of the quadriceps group, it serves to extend the knee joint, moving the lower leg forward. It arises from a series of flat, broad tendons attached to the femur, and attaches to the outer border of the patella.

Vastus medialis.title: Vastus medialis

fields.Latin: musculus vastus medialis or musculus vastus internus
fields.Origin: Medial side of femur
fields.Insertion: Quadriceps tendon
fields.Action: Extends knee

Vastus medialis.summary: The vastus medialis (vastus internus or teardrop muscle) is an extensor muscle located medially in the thigh that extends the knee. The vastus medialis is part of the quadriceps muscle group.

Vastus medialis muscle.title: Vastus medialis

fields.Latin: musculus vastus medialis or musculus vastus internus
fields.Origin: Medial side of femur
fields.Insertion: Quadriceps tendon
fields.Action: Extends knee

Vastus medialis muscle.summary: The vastus medialis (vastus internus or teardrop muscle) is an extensor muscle located medially in the thigh that extends the knee. The vastus medialis is part of the quadriceps muscle group.

Ventral lateral nucleus of thalamus.title: Ventral lateral nucleus
Ventral lateral nucleus of thalamus.summary: The ventral lateral nucleus (VL) is a nucleus in the ventral nuclear group of the thalamus.

Ventral posterior lateral nucleus.title: Ventral posterolateral nucleus
Ventral posterior lateral nucleus.summary: The ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) is one of the subdivisions of the ventral posterior nucleus in the ventral nuclear group of the thalamus. It relays sensory information from second-order neurons of the neospinothalamic tract and the medial lemniscus (of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway), which synapse with third-order neurons in the nucleus. These then project to the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus.

Ventral posterior medial nucleus.title: Ventral posteromedial nucleus
Ventral posterior medial nucleus.summary: The ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) is a nucleus within the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus and serves an analogous somatosensory relay role for the ascending trigeminothalamic tracts as its lateral neighbour the ventral posterolateral nucleus serves for dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway 2nd-order neurons. The term "ventral posteromedial nucleus" was introduced by Le Gros Clark in 1930.

Vertebral artery.title: Vertebral artery

fields.Branches: Basilar artery; Posterior spinal artery; Anterior spinal artery; Posterior inferior cerebellar artery

Vertebral artery.summary: The vertebral arteries are major arteries of the neck. Typically, the vertebral arteries originate from the subclavian arteries. Each vessel courses superiorly along each side of the neck, merging within the skull to form the single, midline basilar artery.

Vertebral vein.title: Vertebral vein
Vertebral vein.summary: The vertebral vein is formed in the suboccipital triangle, from numerous small tributaries which spring from the internal vertebral venous plexuses and issue from the vertebral canal above the posterior arch of the atlas. They unite with small veins from the deep muscles at the upper part of the back of the neck, and form a vessel which enters the foramen in the transverse process of the atlas, and descends, forming a dense plexus around the vertebral artery, in the canal formed by the transverse foramina of the upper six cervical vertebrae. This plexus ends in a single trunk, which emerges from the transverse foramina of the sixth cervical vertebra, and opens at the root of the neck into th

Vestibular nerve.title: Vestibular nerve
Vestibular nerve.summary: The vestibular nerve is one of the two branches of the vestibulocochlear nerve (the cochlear nerve being the other). In humans the vestibular nerve transmits sensory information from vestibular hair cells located in the two otolith organs (the utricle and the saccule) and the three semicircular canals via the vestibular ganglion of Scarpa. Information from the otolith organs reflects gravity and linear accelerations of the head.

Vestibular nuclei.title: Vestibular nuclei
Vestibular nuclei.summary: The vestibular nuclei (VN) are the cranial nuclei for the vestibular nerve located in the brainstem. In Terminologia Anatomica, they are grouped in both the pons and the medulla in the brainstem.

Vestibule.title: Vestibule
Vestibule.summary: Vestibule or vestibulum may refer to:

Vitreous body.title: Vitreous body
Vitreous body.summary: In human anatomy, the vitreous body (from Latin vitreus 'glassy') is the clear gel that fills the space between the lens and the retina of the eye (the vitreous chamber) in humans and other vertebrates. It is often referred to as the vitreous humor (also spelled humour, from Latin meaning 'liquid'), or simply "the vitreous". Vitreous fluid or "liquid vitreous" is the liquid component of the vitreous gel, found after a vitreous detachment.

Vitreous humor.title: Vitreous body
Vitreous humor.summary: In human anatomy, the vitreous body (from Latin vitreus 'glassy') is the clear gel that fills the space between the lens and the retina of the eye (the vitreous chamber) in humans and other vertebrates. It is often referred to as the vitreous humor (also spelled humour, from Latin meaning 'liquid'), or simply "the vitreous". Vitreous fluid or "liquid vitreous" is the liquid component of the vitreous gel, found after a vitreous detachment.

Vocal ligament.title: Vocal cords
Vocal ligament.summary: The vocal cords, also known as vocal folds, are folds of throat tissues that are key in creating sounds through vocalization. The length of the vocal cords affects the pitch of voice, similar to a stringed musical instrument. Open when breathing and vibrating for speech or singing, the folds are controlled via the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve.

Vocalis.title: Thyroarytenoid muscle

fields.Origin: Inner surface of the thyroid cartilage (anterior aspect)
fields.Insertion: Anterior surface of arytenoid cartilage
fields.Innervation: Recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus
fields.Action: Helps to reduce tension on the vocal folds during speech to decrease pitch

Vocalis.summary: The thyroarytenoid muscle is a broad, thin muscle that forms the body of the vocal fold and that supports the wall of the ventricle and its appendix. It functions to shorten the vocal folds.

Vomer.title: Vomer
Vomer.summary: The vomer (; Latin: vomer, lit. 'ploughshare') is one of the unpaired facial bones of the skull. It is located in the midsagittal line, and articulates with the sphenoid, the ethmoid, the left and right palatine bones, and the left and right maxillary bones. The vomer forms the inferior part of the nasal septum in humans, with the superior part formed by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone.

Xiphoid process.title: Xiphoid process
Xiphoid process.summary: The xiphoid process (), also referred to as the ensiform process, xiphisternum, or metasternum, constitutes a small cartilaginous process (extension) located in the inferior segment of the sternum, typically ossified in adult humans. Both the Greek-derived term xiphoid and its Latin equivalent, ensiform, connote a "swordlike" or "sword-shaped" morphology.

Zona incerta.title: Zona incerta
Zona incerta.summary: The zona incerta (ZI) is a horizontally elongated small nucleus that separates the larger subthalamic nucleus from the thalamus. Its connections project extensively over the brain from the cerebral cortex down into the spinal cord. Its function is unknown, though several potential functions related to "limbic–motor integration" have been proposed, such as controlling visceral activity and pain; gating sensory input and synchronizing cortical and subcortical brain rhythms.

Zona orbicularis.title: Zona orbicularis
Zona orbicularis.summary: The zona orbicularis or annular ligament is a ligament on the neck of the femur formed by the circular fibers of the articular capsule of the hip joint. It is also known as the orbicular zone, ring ligament, and zonular band.

Zonular fibres.title: Zonule of Zinn
Zonular fibres.summary: In human anatomy, the zonule of Zinn (; also called the ciliary zonule or Zinn's membrane after Johann Gottfried Zinn) is a ring of fibrous strands forming a zonule (little band) that connects the ciliary body with the crystalline lens of the eye. The Zonular fibers are viscoelastic cables, although their component microfibrils are stiff structures. These fibers are sometimes collectively referred to as the suspensory ligaments of the lens, as they act like suspensory ligaments.

Zygomatic bone.title: Zygomatic bone

fields.Articulations: Maxilla, temporal bone, sphenoid bone and frontal bone

Zygomatic bone.summary: In the human skull, the zygomatic bone (from Ancient Greek: ζῠγόν, romanized: zugón, lit. 'yoke'), also called cheekbone or malar bone, is a paired irregular bone, situated at the upper and lateral part of the face and forming part of the lateral wall and floor of the orbit, of the temporal fossa and the infratemporal fossa. It presents a malar and a temporal surface; four processes (the frontosphenoidal, orbital, maxillary, and temporal), and four borders.

Zygomaticus major muscle.title: Zygomaticus major muscle

fields.Origin: Anterior of zygomatic
fields.Insertion: Modiolus of the mouth
fields.Action: Draws the angle of the mouth upward laterally
fields.Innervation: Zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve

Zygomaticus major muscle.summary: The zygomaticus major muscle is a muscle of the face. It arises from either zygomatic arch (cheekbone); it inserts at the corner of the mouth. It is innervated by branches of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

Zygomaticus minor muscle.title: Zygomaticus minor muscle

fields.Origin: Zygomatic bone
fields.Insertion: Skin of the upper lip
fields.Action: Elevates upper lip

Zygomaticus minor muscle.summary: The zygomaticus minor muscle is a muscle of facial expression. It originates from the zygomatic bone, lateral to the rest of the levator labii superioris muscle, and inserts into the outer part of the upper lip. It draws the upper lip backward, upward, and outward and is used in smiling.

inferior frontal gyrus.title: Inferior frontal gyrus
inferior frontal gyrus.summary: The inferior frontal gyrus (IFG; also gyrus frontalis inferior) is the lowest positioned gyrus of the frontal gyri, of the frontal lobe, and is part of the prefrontal cortex. Its superior border is the inferior frontal sulcus (which divides it from the middle frontal gyrus), its inferior border is the lateral sulcus (which divides it from the superior temporal gyrus) and its posterior border is the inferior precentral sulcus. Above it is the middle frontal gyrus, behind it is the precentral gyrus.

Adductor hallucis.title: Adductor hallucis muscle

fields.Origin: Oblique head: proximal ends of middle 3 metatarsal bones; Transverse head: MTP ligaments of lateral 3 toes
fields.Insertion: Lateral side of base of first phalanx of the 1st toe; sesamoid apparatus
fields.Action: Adducts hallux

Adductor hallucis.summary: The Adductor hallucis (adductor obliquus hallucis) arises by two heads—oblique and transverse and is responsible for adducting the big toe. It has two heads, both are innervated by the lateral plantar nerve.

Adductor pollicis.title: Adductor pollicis muscle

fields.Origin: Transverse head: anterior body of the third metacarpal; Oblique head: bases of the second and the third metacarpals and the adjacent trapezoid and capitate bones
fields.Insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb and the ulnar sesamoid
fields.Action: Adducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint
fields.Antagonist: Abductor pollicis longus muscle, abductor pollicis brevis muscle
fields.Innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (T1)

Adductor pollicis.summary: In human anatomy, the adductor pollicis muscle is a muscle in the hand that functions to adduct the thumb. It has two heads: transverse and oblique. It is a fleshy, flat, triangular, and fan-shaped muscle deep in the thenar compartment beneath the long flexor tendons and the lumbrical muscles at the center of the palm.

Flexor carpi ulnaris.title: Flexor carpi ulnaris muscle

fields.Origin: Medial epicondyle (common flexor tendon) and medial margin on olecranon of ulna
fields.Insertion: Pisiform, hook of the hamate, base of the fifth metacarpal bone (volar aspect)
fields.Innervation: Muscular branches of ulnar nerve (from C8 and T1)
fields.Action: Flexion and adduction of wrist
fields.Antagonist: Extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle and extensor carpi radialis longus muscle

Flexor carpi ulnaris.summary: The flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) is a muscle of the forearm that flexes and adducts at the wrist joint.

Flexor hallucis brevis.title: Flexor hallucis brevis muscle

fields.Origin: Plantar aspect of the cuneiforms, plantar calcaneocuboid ligament, long plantar ligament
fields.Insertion: Medial Head: Medial sesamoid bone of the metatarsophalangeal joint, proximal phalanx of great toe. Lateral head: Lateral sesamoid bone of the metatarsophalangeal joint, proximal phalanx of great toe
fields.Action: Flex hallux

Flexor hallucis brevis.summary: Flexor hallucis brevis muscle is a muscle of the foot that flexes the big toe.

Flexor hallucis longus.title: Flexor hallucis longus muscle

fields.Origin: Fibula, posterior aspect of middle 1/3
fields.Insertion: Plantar surface; base of distal phalanx of hallux
fields.Action: Flexes all joints of the big toe, plantar flexion of the ankle joint
fields.Blood supply: (Muscular branch of peroneal artery (peroneal branch of the posterior tibial artery)

Flexor hallucis longus.summary: The flexor hallucis longus muscle (FHL) attaches to the plantar surface of phalanx of the great toe and is responsible for flexing that toe. The FHL is one of the three deep muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg, the others being the flexor digitorum longus and the tibialis posterior. The tibialis posterior is the most powerful of these deep muscles.

Flexor pollicis brevis.title: Flexor pollicis brevis muscle

fields.Origin: Trapezium, flexor retinaculum
fields.Insertion: Thumb, proximal phalanx
fields.Action: Flexes the thumb at the first metacarpophalangeal joint
fields.Innervation: Recurrent branch of the median nerve, deep branch of ulnar nerve (medial head)

Flexor pollicis brevis.summary: The flexor pollicis brevis is a muscle in the hand that flexes the thumb. It is one of three thenar muscles. It has both a superficial part and a deep part.

Flexor pollicis longus.title: Flexor pollicis longus muscle

fields.Origin: The middle 1/2 of the anterior surface of the radius and adjacent to the interosseus membrane.
fields.Insertion: The base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
fields.Action: Flexion of the thumb
fields.Antagonist: Extensor pollicis longus muscle, extensor pollicis brevis muscle
fields.Innervation: Anterior interosseous nerve (branch of median nerve) (C8, T1)

Flexor pollicis longus.summary: The flexor pollicis longus (; FPL, Latin flexor, bender; pollicis, of the thumb; longus, long) is a muscle in the forearm and hand that flexes the thumb. It lies in the same plane as the flexor digitorum profundus. This muscle is unique to humans, being either rudimentary or absent in other primates.

Flocculus.title: Flocculus
Flocculus.summary: The flocculus (Latin: tuft of wool, diminutive) is a small lobe of the cerebellum at the posterior border of the middle cerebellar peduncle anterior to the biventer lobule. Like other parts of the cerebellum, the flocculus is involved in motor control. It is an essential part of the vestibulo-ocular reflex, and aids in the learning of basic motor skills in the brain.

Fourth metacarpal bone.title: Fourth metacarpal bone
Fourth metacarpal bone.summary: The fourth metacarpal bone (metacarpal bone of the ring finger) is shorter and smaller than the third. The base is small and quadrilateral; its superior surface presents two facets, a large one medially for articulation with the hamate, and a small one laterally for the capitate. On the radial side are two oval facets, for articulation with the third metacarpal; and on the ulnar side a single concave facet, for the fifth metacarpal.

Fourth metatarsal bone.title: Fourth metatarsal bone
Fourth metatarsal bone.summary: The fourth metatarsal bone is a long bone in the foot. It is smaller in size than the third metatarsal bone and is the third longest (and smallest) of the five metatarsal bones. The fourth metatarsal is analogous to the fourth metacarpal bone in the hand As the four other metatarsals bones it can be divided into three parts; base, body and head.

Fourth rib.title: Rib cage
Fourth rib.summary: The rib cage or thoracic cage is an endoskeletal enclosure in the thorax of most vertebrates that comprises the ribs, vertebral column and sternum, which protect the vital organs of the thoracic cavity, such as the heart, lungs and great vessels and support the shoulder girdle to form the core part of the axial skeleton. A typical human thoracic cage consists of 12 pairs of ribs and the adjoining costal cartilages, the sternum (along with the manubrium and xiphoid process), and the 12 thoracic vertebrae articulating with the ribs. The thoracic cage also provides attachments for extrinsic skeletal muscles of the neck, upper limbs, upper abdomen and back, and together with the overlying skin a

Fourth ventricle.title: Fourth ventricle
Fourth ventricle.summary: The fourth ventricle is one of the four connected fluid-filled cavities within the human brain. These cavities, known collectively as the ventricular system, consist of the left and right lateral ventricles, the third ventricle, and the fourth ventricle. The fourth ventricle extends from the cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of Sylvius) to the obex, and is filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

Frontal bone.title: Frontal bone

fields.Articulations: Twelve bones: the sphenoid, the ethmoid, the two parietals, the two nasals, the two maxillae, the two lacrimals, and the two zygomatics

Frontal bone.summary: In the human skull, the frontal bone or sincipital bone is an unpaired bone which consists of two portions. These are the vertically oriented squamous part, and the horizontally oriented orbital part, making up the bony part of the forehead, part of the bony orbital cavity holding the eye, and part of the bony part of the nose respectively. The name comes from the Latin word frons (meaning "forehead").

Frontal branch of superficial temporal a.title: Superficial temporal artery

fields.Branches: Transverse facial artery ; Middle temporal artery ; Anterior auricular branch ; frontal branch ; parietal branch

Frontal branch of superficial temporal a.summary: In human anatomy, the superficial temporal artery is a major artery of the head. It arises from the external carotid artery when it splits into the superficial temporal artery and maxillary artery. Its pulse can be felt above the zygomatic arch, above and in front of the tragus of the ear.

Frontalis muscle.title: Frontalis muscle

fields.Origin: Galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurotis)
fields.Insertion: Orbicularis oculi muscle
fields.Action: Raises eyebrows and wrinkles forehead

Frontalis muscle.summary: The frontalis muscle (from Latin 'frontal muscle') is a muscle which covers parts of the forehead of the skull.
